analysis.one_liner: Requires TV and cable operators to give political candidates free broadcast time.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral; with only 2 cosponsors, it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Communications Act to require television broadcasters and cable operators to hand every qualified political candidate in a statewide or national race at least two hours of free airtime each election year, with much of it in prime time shortly before Election Day. The time would be used for unedited segments where candidates speak directly to voters. A broadcaster that substantially refuses could lose its license renewal; a cable operator that refuses could lose its franchise renewal. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Qualified candidates whose party got more than 2 percent of the vote in the last comparable election would receive free airtime, including in prime evening hours, letting them reach voters without buying ads. Voters would get long, unedited statements directly from candidates instead of only 30-second paid spots. Candidates would be somewhat less dependent on big donors to pay for television advertising.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Candidates and voters, over ad-funded campaigns

how_it_helps.text: Each television station must give every qualified candidate in a statewide or national election at least two hours of free broadcast time each even-numbered year, with at least half airing between 7 p.m. and 10 p.m., at least two-thirds of an election year's allotment in the final two months, and at least half in the final three weeks before Election Day.
The free time must be used for unedited segments in which the candidate speaks directly to the camera, giving voters longer, unfiltered access to candidates than paid 30-second ads.

A candidate qualifies if their party received more than 2 percent of the vote in the most recent statewide or national election, and comparable time must be allotted to candidates for the same office, so incumbents and challengers are treated alike.

Cable operators must provide free time under the same terms as broadcasters, and a station or operator that substantially refuses can lose its license or franchise renewal — the only sanction, so no fines are attached.
The bill explicitly does not restrict paid political advertising, so the free time is an addition, not a substitute, for candidate ad buys.

analysis.who_pays: Television broadcasters and cable operators, who would give up roughly two hours or more per qualified candidate per election year of airtime they currently sell to advertisers, concentrated in the most valuable evening slots. Political advertisers competing for that same prime-time inventory would also face tighter supply.

drawbacks.text: Broadcasters and cable operators lose prime-time inventory they can sell, and the bill caps total free political time at four and a half hours per week with proportionate reductions if more time is required — a real cost in an already shrinking ad market.
The 2 percent vote threshold excludes minor-party and independent candidates who did not meet it in the last election, locking them out of the free time while major-party candidates receive it.

The bill does not limit paid political advertising or the outside spending around it, so big-money campaign ads would continue; free airtime would sit alongside unlimited spending rather than displace it.
The only penalty is non-renewal of a license or franchise, a blunt tool that in practice is rarely used, raising questions about how the requirement would actually be enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but structural: candidates get a guaranteed platform, and voters get unedited candidate messages without those messages being paid for by donors. The cost falls on broadcasters in the form of foregone ad revenue, which is why broadcasters would oppose it, and the enforcement mechanism is weak. The bill leaves paid campaign advertising untouched, so it softens one channel of money in politics without capping spending overall.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the Fairness in Political Advertising Act of 2019 on January 30, 2019, joined by Reps. Eleanor Holmes Norton and Sean Patrick Maloney.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
It attracted only 2 cosponsors in the House, both Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats and 429 total House members at the time of introduction.

Under the bill, broadcasters would have had to allot at least two hours of free time per qualified candidate in statewide and national elections each even-numbered year, and cable operators would have faced parallel obligations, with license or franchise renewal conditioned on compliance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Television broadcasters and cable operators keep the prime-time inventory that the bill would have required them to hand to candidates free of charge, and paid political advertising continues unchanged. Nothing in the record shows any organization lobbying against it; the bill simply never had enough support to move.

for.name: Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred never held a hearing or markup, and no version was ever scheduled for a House floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition is recorded; the only members on record are three Democrats (the sponsor and 2 cosponsors), so the partisan shape of the fight cannot be measured.

industries.note: Stations would have surrendered at least two hours of prime-weighted airtime per qualified candidate each election year, airtime they currently sell to political and commercial advertisers. Broadcasters' interest in stopping the bill was keeping that revenue, which is the same revenue that keeps candidate messaging expensive and donor-dependent.

The bill would have required cable operators to provide free candidate airtime on the same terms as broadcasters, with franchise renewal conditioned on compliance, a parallel cost in sellable inventory.

industries.industry: Political advertising buyers and campaign ad consultants
industries.note: Candidates would have gotten a free guaranteed platform, reducing reliance on paid ads and the consultants and ad markets that profit from them. Paid advertising itself would have continued unrestricted, so the effect on the industry is limited rather than total.
